pul-community-acquired-pneumonia.title: Community-acquired pneumonia
pul-community-acquired-pneumonia.summary: Three days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain with focal crackles with egophony over the right lower lung field is the presentation that defines community-acquired pneumonia. Chest radiography confirms it, and empiric antibiotic therapy guided by a severity score is the initial management.

sections.heading: Overview
paras: Community-acquired pneumonia describes the clinical picture of three days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain produced by alveolar infection with an inflammatory exudate filling the airspaces. The account that follows moves from the underlying process to the bedside picture, then to confirmation and initial treatment — the order in which the problem is usually met.

How often the problem is seen depends on where the counting is done, and case definitions have shifted enough over time that historical series need reading with care. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that site-of-care scoring prevents both risky discharges and unnecessary admissions.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: The process at work is alveolar infection with an inflammatory exudate filling the airspaces. Once that is established, the downstream findings follow in a predictable order, which is what makes the presentation recognisable at the bedside.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes empiric antibiotic therapy guided by a severity score the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: Patients most often describe three days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain, and it is the tempo of that history — how quickly it arrived and whether it is progressing — that carries the diagnostic weight.

Presentations at the extremes of age are frequently less typical, and a normal early course does not exclude the diagnosis. A history of three days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: The sign to look for is focal crackles with egophony over the right lower lung field; it is more specific than the rest of the examination and is worth eliciting carefully.
Interobserver agreement for the classic signs is only moderate, which is a reason to weigh them alongside the history rather than above it.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paras: Chest radiography is the initial study, chosen because it confirms the diagnosis and separates it from the alternatives that present the same way.

pul-chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-diseas.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation
pul-chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-diseas.summary: Two days of worsening dyspnea with increased sputum purulence with diffuse expiratory wheezing with a prolonged expiratory phase is the presentation that defines chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation. sections.heading: Overview
paras: The presentation that names chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation is two days of worsening dyspnea with increased sputum purulence; the process behind it is airway inflammation superimposed on fixed expiratory airflow limitation. The account that follows moves from the underlying process to the bedside picture, then to confirmation and initial treatment — the order in which the problem is usually met.

Prevalence estimates depend heavily on the setting in which they were gathered; referral series and community series describe different populations. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that noninvasive ventilation is the intervention with the clearest mortality benefit in severe episodes.

paras: The process at work is airway inflammation superimposed on fixed expiratory airflow limitation. Tracing the picture back to that single process explains why the individual findings travel together rather than appearing in isolation.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes inhaled bronchodilators, systemic glucocorticoids, and antibiotics when criteria are met the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.
